html:
A castle on flat ground in the middle of Kyoto, built as the Kyoto residence of the Tokugawa shoguns. In 1601 Tokugawa Ieyasu ordered the lords of western Japan to pay for its building, and it was finished in 1626 under his grandson Tokugawa Iemitsu. Parts of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Fushimi Castle were moved here in 1625 and 1626. The shoguns ruled from Edo, now Tokyo, but the emperor's court stayed in Kyoto, and the castle, southwest of the Imperial Palace, was the shogun's foothold in the imperial city.

Two rings of walls and wide moats enclose 27.5 hectares. Between them stands the Ninomaru Palace, six linked buildings of hinoki cypress decorated with gold leaf, carved wood and sliding doors painted by artists of the Kanō school, all meant to show the shogun's power and wealth. The rooms run in order of rank: humble visitors were received in the outer rooms, great ones further in. Its corridors have "nightingale floors" that chirp underfoot, often said to warn of intruders, though the sound comes from clamps rubbing against nails. The garden beside it, with a pond and three islands, was designed by the tea master Kobori Enshū. The five-storey keep burned after a lightning strike in 1750, and the inner palace in a city fire of 1788; the present Honmaru Palace was moved here from the imperial grounds in 1893 and 1894.

In 1867, in the Ninomaru Palace, the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, announced that he was handing power back to the emperor, the step that opened the Meiji Restoration. In 1868 the imperial cabinet was set up in the castle, which became a detached imperial palace, and the Tokugawa hollyhock crest was replaced with the imperial chrysanthemum wherever possible. It was given to the city in 1939, opened to the public in 1940, and is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
